explain.say: Now see the pump. The cell membrane has carrier proteins, tiny pumps that grab a mineral ion outside and carry it across to the inside. This is called active transport: moving things from low to high concentration. Why does that need effort?

faq.q: Why are minerals hard for roots to absorb?
faq.a: The soil water usually has a lower concentration of minerals than the root cells. Diffusion would move them out, so the plant must pump them in against the gradient.
asks: Tell me about few minerals in soil

faq.a: Carrier proteins sit in the cell membrane. Each type grabs a particular particle, such as a nitrate ion, changes shape and releases it on the other side.

faq.q: Why does active transport need energy?
faq.a: It moves particles from a low concentration to a high one, against the natural direction of diffusion. That takes energy, released by respiration in the mitochondria.

faq.q: What is the difference between active transport and diffusion?
faq.a: Diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration and needs no energy. Active transport moves them from low to high and needs energy and carrier proteins.

faq.q: What happens to roots in waterlogged soil?
faq.a: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so root cells cannot respire well and make less energy. Active transport slows down, and the plant can become short of minerals.
asks: Why do plants suffer in flooded soil?

facts: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
Plants absorb mineral ions such as nitrate and magnesium mainly by active transport in root hair cells.

wrong.0: Less energy cannot speed up an energy-hungry process.
wrong.2: Active transport depends directly on energy from respiration.
